question:
Patient note:
A 61-year-old man with a remote history of total laryngectomy for T3 squamous-cell carcinoma of the larynx, chronic atrial fibrillation on rate control (no anticoagulant by patient preference), and insulin-dependent type 2 diabetes was brought to the emergency department by his home health nurse after she found him on the bedroom floor next to his powered wheelchair roughly thirty minutes before arrival; according to her report he was gesturing for help but produced no sound and appeared dyspneic, so emergency medical services were summoned. Paramedics state that on scene he was breathing spontaneously through his permanent tracheostomy stoma, had a portable electrolarynx lying unused on the nightstand, displayed no signs of seizure activity, and had a capillary glucose of 108 mg/dL; no medications were administered en route apart from 2 L/min supplemental oxygen through a tracheostomy collar. On entry to the resuscitation bay the patient is supine, eyes already open and tracking personnel purposefully as the stretcher is positioned, blinking normally and shifting gaze between speakers without any external prompting. Airway inspection reveals a mature 1.5 cm tracheostoma with a cuffless, nonfenestrated tube in place; humidification collar delivering 28 % FiO₂ is connected and misting appropriately. He is unable to phonate by design of his altered anatomy, and no guttural sounds, moans, or whispers are produced even when repeatedly asked to state his name; instead he mouths words silently, nods or shakes his head, and writes short phrases on a clipboard handed to him. Vital signs obtained prior to any emergency department intervention are temperature 37.2 °C orally, heart rate 96 beats/min and irregularly irregular, blood pressure 138/78 mm Hg in the right brachial artery, respiratory rate 22 breaths/min with modest accessory muscle use, and oxygen saturation 94 % on the aforementioned trach collar. Pupils measure 3 mm bilaterally and are briskly reactive to light; extraocular movements are intact and conjugate without nystagmus. Facial symmetry is preserved and corneal reflexes present. Cranial nerve testing otherwise demonstrates intact eyebrow raise, eyelid closure, and shoulder shrug on request. When instructed—using gestures and written prompts—the patient purposefully squeezes the examiner’s fingers, releases upon command, lifts each arm to 90 degrees, wiggles fingers, flexes hips against gravity, and plantar-flexes as directed, all without delay or drift; no abnormal posturing, spasticity, or flaccidity is noted. Sensory examination shows intact light-touch appreciation in all extremities; rapid alternating movements are slightly slowed on the right, consistent with prior baseline according to the nurse. Deep tendon reflexes are 2+ and symmetric, and plantar responses are downgoing. He blinks twice in response to “blink twice if you can feel this” when the examiner lightly pinches the extensor surface of his left forearm, confirming comprehension. Skin survey reveals a well-healed midline neck scar, no fresh trauma, and warm, well-perfused extremities with capillary refill under two seconds. Cardiac auscultation detects an irregularly irregular rhythm without murmurs, rubs, or gallops; lung fields are clear to auscultation bilaterally with coarse air movement near the stoma but no wheezes or crackles. Abdomen is soft, nontender, and nondistended; bowel sounds are present. Peripheral pulses are 2+ in all limbs, and there is no lower-extremity edema. Point-of-care arterial blood gas sampled on the trach collar prior to any manipulation shows pH 7.37, PaCO₂ 43 mm Hg, PaO₂ 76 mm Hg, bicarbonate 24 mEq/L, and base excess 0 mEq/L. Bedside chemistry panel reveals sodium 138 mEq/L, potassium 4.0 mEq/L, chloride 101 mEq/L, bicarbonate 25 mEq/L, blood urea nitrogen 20 mg/dL, creatinine 1.1 mg/dL, and glucose 106 mg/dL. Hematocrit measures 39 %, white blood cell count 7.8 × 10⁹/L, and platelet count 238 × 10⁹/L. Coagulation profile shows INR 1.1 and aPTT 32 seconds. No sedative, paralytic, or analgesic agents have been administered prior to this assessment, and he denies (by head shake) any ingestion of alcohol, opioids, or illicit substances today. Home medications include metoprolol tartrate 25 mg twice daily, insulin glargine 22 units nightly with sliding scale lispro, and atorvastatin 20 mg nightly; the visiting nurse confirms adherence. Last insulin dose was the previous evening. Family history is notable only for coronary artery disease in a sibling. The patient lives alone, communicates normally with an electrolarynx, and is fully independent in activities of daily living; no previous cerebrovascular events are documented. At this point his mental status appears intact, he maintains eye contact without external stimulus, follows every written or gestured instruction accurately, yet remains completely silent due to anatomical absence of the vocal apparatus.

Question: What is the patient's Glasgow Coma Score? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
The Glasgow Coma Scale assesses the best eye (1–4), verbal (1–5), and motor (1–6) responses. At presentation:
- Eyes: already open without stimulation, E4.
- Verbal: no audible words or sounds. For a forced numeric score, record V1; clinically, the component is not testable because of laryngectomy, not impaired consciousness.
- Motor: squeezes and releases the examiner’s fingers on command, M6.
Under the numeric convention, E4 + V1 + M6 = 11. The anatomical limitation should accompany the score.
Final answer: 11
